justification_text:
My point estimates across all three horizons reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with only modest upward drift. For the one-day estimate, I anchored heavily on the most recent observed price level, assuming mean-reverting behavior over such a short window with minimal drift. The slight upward nudge in the one-week and one-month estimates reflects a mild positive trend assumption — perhaps driven by underlying fundamental factors such as gradual demand growth, cost-push pressures, or a slightly bullish macro backdrop — but the magnitude of drift I assumed was deliberately small, given the absence of strong directional signals.

The confidence interval widths expand meaningfully as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the standard principle that uncertainty compounds over time. For the one-day interval, I drew on typical intraday or session-to-session volatility, which tends to be relatively contained. By the one-week horizon, I incorporated the possibility of scheduled data releases, geopolitical developments, or supply-side surprises that could shift sentiment. The one-month interval is wide enough to capture a broader range of macro scenarios, including shifts in monetary policy expectations, changes in demand conditions, or structural supply disruptions — all of which become more plausible over a longer window.

There are several tail risks that could push outcomes well outside my stated intervals in either direction. On the upside, a sudden supply shock — such as geopolitical disruption to key production or transport routes — or stronger-than-expected demand data could drive prices meaningfully above the upper bounds I cited. On the downside, a sharp deterioration in global growth expectations, a surprise demand destruction event, or aggressive policy intervention could push prices below my lower bounds. Liquidity conditions and speculative positioning also matter; if crowded trades unwind rapidly, volatility could spike far beyond what historical norms would suggest, rendering even the one-day interval too narrow.
